Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 29, verses 1–3:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It is entirely Meccan according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Jabir. It is entirely Medinan according to one of the two opinions attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and according to Qatadah. According to the other opinion attributed to them both, which is the view of Yahya ibn Sallam, it is Meccan except for its first ten verses, which were revealed in Medina concerning those Muslims who were in Mecca. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: it was revealed between Mecca and Medina. It has sixty-nine verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Do people think that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and they will not be tested? And We certainly tested those before them, so Allah will surely make known those who are truthful and will surely make known the liars.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ The discussion of the opening letters of the surahs has already passed. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is "I am Allah, the All-Knowing." It has also been said that it is the name of the surah, and that "Qur'an" is the name of the whole Book.

"Hasiba" (did... think) is an interrogative used for affirmation and rebuke, and its meaning is "thought" (zann). "An yutraku" (that they be left) is in the accusative position, governed by "hasiba," and it together with its verb takes the place of the two objects according to the opinion of Sibawayh. The second "an" in "an yaqulu" (that they say) is in the accusative position in one of two ways: either with the meaning of "li-an yaqulu" (for that they say), or "bi-an yaqulu" (by that they say), or "'ala an yaqulu" (on condition that they say). The other way is that it is in apposition by repetition, the sense being: "Do people think that they will be left alone — did they think that they would say, 'We believe,' while they are not tested?"

Ibn 'Abbas and others said: by "the people" he means a group of believers who were in Mecca, and the unbelievers of Quraysh were harming them and punishing them for Islam. Among them were Salamah ibn Hisham, 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn al-Walid, 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Yasir (his father), Sumayyah (his mother), a number of the Banu Makhzum and others. Their hearts would be distressed by this, and it would sometimes be considered strange that Allah should give the unbelievers power over the believers. Mujahid and others said: this verse was revealed to console them and to inform them that this is the way of Allah with His servants, a test and a trial for the believers.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: although this verse was revealed for this cause or for what is similar in meaning to it, its ruling remains among the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and its judgment persists for the rest of time. This is because the trial from Allah, may He be exalted, remains on the frontiers of the Muslims through captivity, the inflicting of harm by the enemy, and other things. Likewise, if one considers every place, there is trial in it through sicknesses and various kinds of afflictions. But what most resembles the situation of the Muslims with Quraysh is what we have mentioned concerning the enemy on every frontier. I (al-Qurtubi) say: how excellent is what he said, and he spoke truly, may Allah be pleased with him.

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Mihja', the freed slave of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who was the first Muslim to be killed on the day of Badr. 'Amir ibn al-Hadrami shot him with an arrow and killed him. On that day the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The master of the martyrs is Mihja', and he is the first of this community to be called to the gate of Paradise." His two parents and his wife grieved over him, and then this verse was revealed: "Alif. Lam. Mim. Do people think that they will be left alone..."

Al-Sha'bi said: the opening of this surah was revealed concerning some people among the Muslims who were in Mecca. The Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to them from al-Hudaybiyah that the profession of Islam would not be accepted from them until they emigrated. So they set out, and the polytheists pursued them and harmed them. Then this verse was revealed concerning them: "Alif. Lam. Mim. Do people think that they will be left alone..." They wrote to them: "A verse such-and-such has been revealed concerning you." They said: "We will go out, and if anyone follows us, we will fight him." The polytheists pursued them and fought them; some of them were killed and some of them escaped, and then there was revealed concerning them: ﴿Then indeed your Lord — for those who emigrated after they had been tried...﴾ "And they will not be tested" means they will not be examined. That is, did those who grew distressed at the harm of the polytheists think that they would be satisfied with their merely saying, "We are believers," without being tested in their faith, their selves and their wealth, by means of which the reality of their faith would be made clear?

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We certainly tested those before them﴾, meaning: We tried those who passed before them, such as the Friend (Abraham), who was thrown into the fire, and such as the people who were sawn apart with saws for the religion of Allah, yet they did not turn back from it. Al-Bukhari related from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who said: "We complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was reclining on a cloak of his in the shade of the Ka'bah, and we said to him: 'Will you not seek victory for us? Will you not supplicate for us?' He said: 'Those before you were taken, a man would be placed in a pit dug in the earth, and a saw would be brought and placed on his head, and he would be split in two, and his flesh and bones would be combed with iron combs, yet that would not turn him from his religion. By Allah, this matter will indeed be completed, until a rider travels from San'a' to Hadramawt fearing none but Allah and the wolf concerning his sheep, but you are hasty.'"

Ibn Majah related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "I entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was feverish, so I placed my hand on him and found his heat between my hands over the quilt. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how severe it is upon you!' He said: 'Thus indeed trial is doubled for us, and the reward is doubled for us.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which of the people is most severely tested?' He said: 'The prophets.' I said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Then the righteous. Indeed one of them may be tested with poverty to the extent that he finds nothing but a cloak which he cuts open [[The word occurs in Sunan Ibn Majah with the unpointed "ha," and its marginal note says: "yahuwwabuha" from "habba" with an unpointed "ha" and a single "ba," meaning he makes a collar for it. It occurs in al-Jami' al-Saghir of al-Suyuti with the "jim," and its commentator says: it is with a "jim," a "waw" and a "ha," meaning he tears it and cuts it, and anything whose middle has been cut is "mujawwab." The reading of al-Jami' al-Saghir is the more evident.]] and one of them may rejoice in trial as one of you rejoices in ease.'"

And Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas related: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which of the people is most severely tested?' He said: 'The prophets, then the best and then those next best. A man is tested according to the measure of his religion. If he is firm in his religion, his trial is intensified; and if there is softness in his religion, he is tested according to the measure of his religion. The trial does not cease to be upon the servant until he leaves him walking upon the earth with no sin upon him.'"

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd related that Jesus, peace be upon him, had a minister. One day he rode out and a beast of prey seized him and devoured him. Jesus said: "O Lord, my minister in Your religion, my helper against the Children of Israel, and my successor among them, You gave power over him to a dog, and it devoured him." He said: "Yes, he had with Me a lofty station which his deeds did not reach, so I tested him with this that he might attain that station."

Wahb said: "I read in the book of a man among the disciples: When the path of trial is taken with you, then be glad, for indeed the path of the prophets and the righteous has been taken with you; and when the path of ease is taken with you, then weep over yourself, for indeed you have been turned away from their path."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so Allah will surely make known those who are truthful﴾, meaning: so Allah will surely see those who are truthful in their faith. This meaning has already passed in "al-Baqarah" and elsewhere. Al-Zajjaj said: "That He may know the truthfulness of the truthful by the occurrence of their truthfulness from them, though He had known the truthful from the liar before He created them. But the intent is the occurrence of knowledge regarding what He will requite. He knows the truthfulness of the truthful as something that will come to be, and He knew that it would come to be."

Al-Nahhas said: in this there are two opinions. One is that "saduqu" (they were truthful) is derived from "al-sidq" (truthfulness), and "al-kadhibin" (the liars) is derived from "al-kadhib" (lying), which is the opposite of truthfulness, and the meaning would be: Allah will make clear those who were truthful, who said, "We are believers," and held the same belief, and those who lied when they held otherwise. The other opinion is that "saduqu" is derived from "al-sidq," which means firmness and steadfastness, and "al-kadhibin" is derived from "kadhaba" when it means to have fled. Then the meaning would be: Allah will know those who stood firm in battle, and those who fled, just as the poet said [[He is Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma. "Athar" with a shadda on the "tha'" is the name of a place.]]:

A lion at Athar hunts men, when
the lion lies (flees) from his peers, he is truthful (stands firm).

So he made "la-ya'lamanna" (He will surely know) to be used metaphorically in the place of "fa-la-yubayyinanna" (He will surely make clear).

The reading of the majority is "fa-la-ya'lamanna" with a fatha on the "ya'" and the "lam." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read it with a damma on the "ya'" and a kasra on the "lam," and this reading explains the meaning that al-Nahhas stated. It admits of three meanings. The first is that in the Hereafter He will make these truthful and these liars know their stations of reward and punishment and their deeds in this world, meaning that He will cause them to stand before what they did. The third is that this is from "al-'alamah" (the sign), that is, He will place for each group a sign by which it becomes known. The verse, according to this, looks to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever keeps a secret within himself, Allah will clothe him in its garment."

A lion at Athar hunts men, when

So he made "la-ya'lamanna" (He will surely know) to be used metaphorically in the place of "fa-la-yubayyinanna" (He will surely make clear).

The reading of the majority is "fa-la-ya'lamanna" with a fatha on the "ya'" and the "lam." The third is that this is from "al-'alamah" (the sign), that is, He will place for each group a sign by which it becomes known. The verse, according to this, looks to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever keeps a secret within himself, Allah will clothe him in its garment."

The Exalted said: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they can outrun Us?﴾ That is, shirk. He said: (that they can outstrip us), i.e., escape us and render us powerless before we seize them for what they do. Ibn Abbas said: He means al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl, al-Aswad, al-As ibn Hisham, Shayba, Utba, al-Walid ibn Utba, Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, Handhala ibn Abi Sufyan, and al-As ibn Wa'il.

The Exalted said: (Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah, then indeed the term of Allah is coming). "Yarju" (hopes) here means "fears," from the words of al-Hudhali describing a honey-gatherer:

When the bees stung him, he did not fear their sting
[The line continues: ..
and he allied with her in a house, the bees' comb.
Another version has: 'awasil' (bees).]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 29, verse 8–9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾. It was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, as related by al-Tirmidhi. He said: "Four verses were revealed concerning me," and he mentioned a story. Umm Sa'd said: "Has not God commanded righteousness? By God, I will not eat any food nor drink any drink until I die or you disbelieve." He said: "So when they wanted to feed her, they forced open her mouth (shajaru faha) [shajaru faha: meaning they inserted a stick into a tree so that they could pry her mouth open with it]. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾, to the end of the verse." Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a hadith that is hasan sahih." It is also related from Sa'd that he said: "I was dutiful to my mother, then I embraced Islam. She said: 'You must abandon your religion, or I will neither eat nor drink until I die, and you will be reproached for me, and it will be said, O slayer of his mother!' She remained a day and a day. I said: 'O mother! If you had a hundred souls, and they departed one soul after another, I would not abandon this religion of mine. So if you wish, eat, and if you wish, do not eat.' When she saw that, she ate, and this was revealed: ﴿But if they strive with you that you associate with Me what you have no knowledge of﴾, to the end of the verse."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was revealed concerning 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, the maternal brother of Abu Jahl, and his mother had done the same thing." And also from him: "It was revealed concerning the whole community, for none endures the trial of God except a sincere believer (siddiq)."

As for "husnan" (kindness), it is in the accusative according to the Basran grammarians by way of repetition, meaning "and We enjoined him with kindness." It was also said that it is in the accusative of the cognate or qualifying type (qat'), its estimate being "and We enjoined him with goodness," just as you say "wassaituhu khayran," meaning "with good." The Kufan grammarians said: its estimate is "and We enjoined man that he should do good (husnan)," so a verb is supposed. A poet said:

I marvelled at Dahma'a when they complained of us,
and at the father of Dahma'a when he enjoins us
(to do) good to them, as if they feared us.

That is, he enjoins us that we do good to them, like His saying: "So he began to wipe (fatifiqa mashan)," meaning he wiped, wiping. It was also said: its estimate is "and We enjoined him a matter possessing goodness," so the attribute is put in place of the qualified noun, the modified noun is deleted, and the modifying noun is put in its place. It was also said: its meaning is "We obligated him to goodness."

The common reading is "husnan," with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the sin. Abu Raja', Abu al-'Aliya and al-Dahhak read it with a fatha on the ha' and the sin. Al-Jahdari read "ihsanan" as a verbal noun (masdar), and likewise it is in the codex of Ubayy, the estimate being: "And We enjoined man that he should be kind to them, kindness," and it is not governed by "wassayna," because it has already fulfilled its two objects.

﴿To Me is your return﴾: this is a threat regarding obedience to the parents in the sense of disbelief.

﴿So I will inform you of what you used to do. And those who believed and did righteous deeds – We will surely admit them among the righteous﴾. God, exalted is He, repeated the example of the state of the believers who act righteously, to move souls toward attaining their ranks. His saying "We will surely admit them among the righteous" is an intensification in meaning: those who are at the utmost end of righteousness and its farthest limit. When this ruling is attained by the believer, its fruit and its reward are obtained, which is Paradise.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among people is one who says, "We believe in Allah," but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the trial of people as if it were the punishment of Allah﴾ – the verse. It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who used to say, "We believe in Allah." (When he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the trial of people) i.e., their harm, (as the punishment of Allah) in the Hereafter, so he apostatizes from his faith. It was also said: he panics at that, just as one panics at the punishment of Allah, and does not endure harm suffered for the sake of Allah.

(And if there comes) to the believers (a victory from your Lord, they will surely say) those apostates (“Indeed, we were with you”), and they are liars. So Allah says to them (“Is not Allah most knowing of what is within the breasts of the worlds?”), meaning: Allah knows better than they themselves what is in their breasts. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning people who believed with their tongues, and when a affliction from Allah or a calamity befell them in their persons, they were tried. Al-Dahhak said: It was revealed concerning some hypocrites in Makkah who used to believe, but when they were harmed, they returned to polytheism. Ikrimah said: There were some people who had embraced Islam, but the polytheists compelled them to go out with them to Badr, and some of them were killed. So Allah revealed, "Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves..." The Muslims of Madinah wrote this to the Muslims in Makkah, and they went out, and the polytheists overtook them, and some of them were tried; so this verse was revealed concerning them. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, who embraced Islam and emigrated, then he was harmed and beaten, and he apostatized. He was tortured by Abu Jahl and al-Harith, who were his maternal brothers. Ibn Abbas said: He lived for a long time after that, and his Islam became good.

(And Allah will surely make known those who believed, and He will surely make known the hypocrites.) Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning the group whom the polytheists returned to Makkah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 29, verse 12–13:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Follow our way"﴾, i.e., our religion (din).

(Wal-nahmil khatayakum) is in the jussive mood as a command. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: it is a command with the meaning of a conditional and its response, i.e., "If you follow our way, we will bear your sins," just as the poet said [[The verse is by Mudathar ibn Shaiban al-Namari, and before it is: "My beloved said, when we were afflicted, 'The sons of al-Qarm al-Hijan will overtake us.'"]]:

So I said, "Call, and I will call, for indeed the more lofty of two callers..." to the sound that is called out to.

That is, if you call, I will call. Al-Mahdawi said: The occurrence of "indeed they are liars" after it is by way of taking the meaning into account, because the meaning is, "If you follow our way, we will bear your sins." Since the command in meaning returns to a statement, the denial falls upon it just as a statement would fall upon it. Mujahid said: The polytheists of Quraysh said, "We and you will not be resurrected; so if there is a burden upon you, it is upon us," i.e., we will bear for you what is incumbent upon you. The "bearing" here means taking on responsibility (hamalah), not carrying on the back. It is narrated that the one who said this was al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

(And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens) meaning what is laid upon them of the evil deeds of those whom they wronged, after their good deeds have run out. Its meaning has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it has been discussed earlier in "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 275 and following, first or second edition.]]. Abu Umamah al-Bahili said: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, having many good deeds, and retribution will continue to be taken from him until his good deeds are exhausted. Then he will be called to account, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will say, 'Take retribution from My servant,' and the angels will say, 'No good deeds remain for him.' He will say, 'Take from the evil deeds of the wronged and place them upon him.'" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited, "And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens." Qatadah said: Whoever calls to misguidance will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it, and nothing will be reduced from their burdens. A parallel to this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That they may bear their full burdens on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾. A parallel to this is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it after him, without anything being reduced from their burdens." It is narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurairah and others. Al-Hasan said that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever calls to guidance, and it is followed and acted upon, he has a reward like the rewards of those who follow him, without that diminishing their rewards in any way. And whoever calls to misguidance, and it is followed and acted upon after him, upon him is a burden like the burdens of those who act upon it from among those who follow him, without that diminishing their burdens in any way." Then al-Hasan recited, "And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens." I say: This is a mursal report, and it is the meaning of the hadith of Abu Hurairah, which Muslim narrated. The text of the hadith of Anas ibn Malik from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is that he said: "Whoever calls to misguidance and it is followed, he has a burden like the burdens of those who follow him, without that diminishing their burdens in any way. And whoever calls to guidance and it is followed, he has a reward like the rewards of those who follow him, without that diminishing their rewards in any way." Ibn Majah narrated it in the Sunan. On this topic there are also reports from Abu Juhayfah and Jarir. It has been said: the intended meaning is the helpers of tyrants. It has also been said: the people of innovations when they are followed in them. And it has been said: the originators of new practices when they are acted upon after them. The meanings are close, and the hadith encompasses all of that.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 29, verses 14–15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years﴾. He mentioned the story of Noah as a consolation to His Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: the prophets before you were tested by the disbelievers and they were patient. He singled out Noah for mention because he was the first messenger sent to the earth when it had become filled with disbelief, as its explanation has preceded in "Hud" [See vol. 9, p. 42 and what follows, first or second edition]. And no prophet encountered from his people what Noah encountered, as has preceded in "Hud," from al-Hasan. It is related from Qatadah, from Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first prophet sent was Noah." Qatadah said: "And he was sent from al-Jazirah."

The length of his life has been disputed. It was said: the length of his life is what Allah Exalted mentioned in His Book. Qatadah said: He remained among them before he called them for three hundred years, and he called them for three hundred years, and he remained after the Flood for three hundred and fifty years. Ibn Abbas said: Noah was sent at forty years of age, and he remained among his people a thousand years less fifty years, and he lived after the drowning sixty years, until people multiplied and spread. Also from him: that he was sent when he was two hundred and fifty years old, and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty, and he lived after the Flood two hundred years. Wahb said: Noah lived one thousand and four hundred years. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Noah remained among his people a thousand years less fifty years, and he lived after the Flood seventy years, so the total length of his life was one thousand and twenty years. Awn ibn Shaddad said: Noah was sent when he was three hundred and fifty years old, and he remained among his people a thousand years less fifty years, and he lived after the Flood three hundred and fifty years, so the total length of his life was one thousand six hundred and fifty years. Similar to this is related from al-Hasan.

Al-Hasan said: When the Angel of Death came to Noah to seize his soul, he said: "O Noah, how long have you lived in the world?" He said: "Three hundred years before I was sent, and a thousand years less fifty in my people, and three hundred and fifty years after the Flood." The Angel of Death said: "How did you find the world?" Noah said: "Like a house that has two doors: I entered through this one and I left through that one."

It is related from the hadith of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah sent Noah to his people, He sent him when he was two hundred and fifty years old, and he remained among his people a thousand years less fifty years, and he remained after the Flood two hundred and fifty years. When the Angel of Death came to him, he said: 'O Noah, O greatest of the prophets, O longest-lived, O one whose supplication is answered, how did you find the world?' He said: 'Like a man for whom a house was built, which has two doors: he entered from one and left from the other.'" It has also been said: he entered from one of them, sat for a little while, then left through the other door.

Ibn al-Wardi said: Noah built a house of reeds. It was said to him: "If only you had built other than this." He said: "This is too much for one who is going to die." Abu al-Muhajir said: Noah remained among his people a thousand years less fifty years in a house of hair (a tent of goats' hair). It was said to him: "O Prophet of Allah, build a house." He said: "I will die today [or] I will die tomorrow."

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Five hundred years passed over Noah during which he did not approach women, out of fear of death.

Muqatil and Juwaybir said: When Adam, peace be upon him, became old and his bones grew frail, he said: "O Lord, until when will I struggle and strive?" He said: "O Adam, until a child is born to you circumcised." So Noah was born to him after ten generations, and he was then one thousand years less sixty years old. Some said: less forty years. And Allah knows best.

Noah was the son of Lamak, son of Matushlakh, son of Idris, who is Akhnukh, son of Yard, son of Mahla'il, son of Qaynan, son of Anush, son of Shith, son of Adam. Noah's name was al-Sakan. He was named al-Sakan because people after Adam found tranquility (sakanu) in him, so he is their father. Sam, Ham and Yafith were born to him: Sam begot the Arabs, the Persians and the Romans, and in all of these there is good. Ham begot the Copts, the Sudanese and the Berbers. Yafith begot the Turks, the Slavs, and Gog and Magog. None of these has good in them. Ibn Abbas said: among the descendants of Sam there is whiteness and brown complexion; among the descendants of Ham there is blackness and a little whiteness; among the descendants of Yafith, who are the Turks and the Slavs, there is yellowness and redness. He had a fourth son, Kan'an, who drowned, and the Arabs call him Yam.

Noah was named Noah because he wailed (naha) over his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them to Allah Exalted; when they disbelieved, he wept and wailed over them.

Al-Qushayri Abu al-Qasim Abd al-Karim mentioned in his book al-Tahbir: It is related that Noah, peace be upon him, was named Yashkur, but because of the abundance of his weeping over his sin, Allah revealed to him: "O Noah, how long will you wail?" So he was named Noah. It was asked: "O Messenger of Allah, what was his sin?" He said: "He passed by a dog and said to himself, 'How ugly it is.' So Allah revealed to him: 'You create something more beautiful than this.'" Yazid al-Raqqashi said: He was named Noah only because of how long he wailed over himself.

If it is asked: why did He say "a thousand years less fifty years" and not "nine hundred and fifty years"? There are two answers to this. The first: the intent is to magnify the number, so mentioning "a thousand" is greater in wording and greater in number. The second: it is related that he was given a life span of a thousand years, and he gave fifty years of his life to some of his offspring. When death approached him, he sought to complete the thousand. So Allah Exalted mentioned this as an alert that the deficiency came from his side.

(So the Flood seized them.) Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: the rain. Al-Dahhak: the drowning. It was said: death. This was related by A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, from the Prophet (ﷺ). From this is the saying of the poet:

"The flood of a sweeping death destroyed them."

Al-Nahhas said: Any great thing that encompasses everything, whether of rain, killing or death, is called a tufan (flood).

(While they were wrongdoers.) A clause in the position of a circumstantial state (hal). "A thousand years" is in the accusative as an adverbial of time (zarf). "Less fifty years" is in the accusative as an exception from an affirmative statement (istithna' min al-mujab). According to Sibawayh, it is in the position of the object, because it is dispensed with, like the object. As for al-Mubarrad, Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid, it is for him a pure object, as if you said: "I excepted Zayd."

Note: Hassan ibn Ghalib ibn Najih Abu al-Qasim al-Misri narrated to us: Malik ibn Anas narrated to us from al-Zuhri, from Ibn al-Musayyib, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jibril used to discuss with me the excellence of Umar. I said: 'O Jibril, how far does the excellence of Umar reach?' He said to me: 'O Muhammad, if I had remained with you as long as Noah remained among his people, I would not have conveyed to you the excellence of Umar.'" Al-Khatib Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Thabit al-Baghdadi mentioned it, and said: Hassan ibn Ghalib alone transmitted it from Malik, and it is not established from his hadith.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We saved him and the companions of the ship﴾, is conjoined to the pronoun (the ha').

(And We made it a sign for the worlds.) The pronoun ha' and the alif in "made it" refer either to the ship, or to the punishment, or to the salvation: three opinions.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 29, verses 20–25:**

Allah's statement: ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth"﴾, meaning: say to them, O Muhammad (ﷺ), "Travel through the earth" (**fa-nzuru kayfa bada'a al-khalq**), "and see how He originated creation," despite its multitude, the variety of its forms, the differences of its languages, colours and natures. "And look at the dwellings of the earlier generations, their homes and their remains, and how He destroyed them," so that you may know by that the perfection of Allah's power.

(Then Allah produces the final creation.) Abu Amr and Ibn Kathir read *al-nash'ah* with a fatha on the shin, and both are dialectal variants, like *al-ra'fah* and *al-ra'afah* and similar pairs. Al-Jawhari said: "Anshaʾahu Allah" means He created him, and the noun is *al-nash'ah* and *al-nasha'ah* (with the long vowel), transmitted from Abu Amr ibn al-Ala'.

﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent. He punishes whom He wills﴾, meaning: by His justice.

﴿And has mercy on whom He wills﴾, meaning: by His grace.

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, meaning: you will be brought back and sent back.

﴿You cannot escape [Him] within the earth or within the sky﴾. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "nor those in the sky, [as those who can escape] Allah." This is obscure in Arabic because the pronoun is not expressed in the second part. It is like the verse of Hassan:

"Whoever among you satirises the Messenger of God,
and praises him and supports him, is equal [in this]."

He meant: "and whoever praises him and supports him is equal," so *man* (whoever) was elided. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said the same. A parallel is His statement: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾, meaning: "none of us but he who has a known station." The sense is that the people of the earth cannot overpower Allah on the earth, nor can the people of heaven, if they disobey Him. Qutrub said: "nor in the sky, even if you were in it," as you say: "So-and-so will not escape me in Basra, nor here," meaning: he will not escape me in Basra even if he goes there. It was also said: they cannot flee in the earth or in the sky. Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is "nor whoever is in the sky," with *man* being indefinite rather than relative, and *fi al-sama'* being an adjective to it, with the adjective standing in place of the noun modified. Ibn Sulayman rejected this and said: it is not permissible. He said: when *man* is indefinite it must be described, and its description functions like a relative clause, and it is not permissible to omit the relative pronoun and leave out the clause. He said: the meaning is that people were addressed in what they understand, and the sense is: "even if you were in the sky, you would not frustrate Allah," as He said: ﴿Even if you were in fortified towers﴾.

﴿And you have not, besides Allah, any protector or helper﴾. It is also permissible to read *nasir* with a *raf'* on account of its position, and then *min* is extra.

﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and in His meeting﴾, meaning: in the Qur'an, or in the proofs and signs He has set up.

﴿Those have despaired of My mercy﴾, meaning: of Paradise. The despair is attributed to them, while the meaning is that they were made to despair (*uwisu*). These verses are an interjection from Allah, Most High, as a reminder and warning to the people of Makkah. Then the discourse returned to the story of Abraham, and He said: ﴿So there was not the answer of his people﴾, when he called them to Allah, Most High, ﴿except that they said: "Kill him or burn him."﴾ Then they agreed to burn him. ﴿But Allah saved him from the fire﴾, meaning: from its harm. ﴿Indeed in that﴾, meaning: in his being saved from the great fire, so that it did not burn him after he had been cast into it, ﴿are signs.﴾

The common reading is *jawaba* with a fatha on the ba', as the predicate of *kana*, with *an qalu* in the position of the subject of *kana*. Salim al-Aftas and Amr ibn Dinar read *jawabu* with a damma, as the subject of *kana*, with *inna* in the position of the predicate in the accusative.

﴿And [Abraham] said: "You have only taken idols besides Allah as an affection between you in the worldly life."﴾ Hafs and Hamza read *mawaddata baynikum*. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i read *mawaddatu baynikum*. Al-A'sha, from Abu Bakr, from Asim, and Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read *mawaddatun baynakum*. The rest read *mawaddatu baynakum*. As for the reading of Ibn Kathir, it has three possible analyses, two of which al-Zajjaj mentioned. The first: *mawaddah* is in the nominative as the predicate of *inna*, and *ma* is in the sense of *alladhi*. The sense is: "Indeed that which you have taken besides Allah as idols is an affection between you." The second: it is nominative by an elided subject, meaning: "it is an affection," or "that is an affection between you." The meaning is: your gods, or your community, are an affection between you. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 29, verse 26–27:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾. Lot was the first to affirm Abraham when he saw the fire become for him "coolness and safety." Ibn Ishaq said: Lot believed in Abraham, and he was the son of his sister, and Sarah, who was the daughter of his paternal uncle, also believed in him.

(And he said: "Indeed, I am emigrating to my Lord.") Al-Nakha'i and Qatadah said: The one who said, "Indeed, I am emigrating to my Lord," was Abraham, peace be upon him. Qatadah said: He emigrated from Kutha, which is a village in the outskirts of Kufa, to Harran and then to Syria, and with him was his nephew Lot son of Haran son of Terah, and his wife Sarah. Al-Kalbi said: He emigrated from the land of Harran to Palestine, and he was the first to emigrate from the land of disbelief. Muqatil said: Abraham emigrated when he was seventy-five years old. It was also said: The one who said, "Indeed, I am emigrating to my Lord," was Lot, peace be upon him. Al-Bayhaqi mentioned from Qatadah that he said: The first to emigrate to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with his family was Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him. Qatadah said: I heard Al-Nadr ibn Anas say: I heard Abu Hamza, meaning Anas ibn Malik, say: Uthman ibn Affan went out with Ruqayyah, the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to the land of Abyssinia, and news of them was delayed from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then a woman from Quraysh came and said: "O Muhammad, I saw your son-in-law and his wife with him." He said: "In what condition did you see them?" She said: "I saw him carrying his wife on a donkey from this *dabbabah*" [[That is, the weak ones who walk slowly and do not hasten.]] "and he was driving her." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah keep them company. Indeed, Uthman is the first to emigrate with his family after Lot." Al-Bayhaqi said: This refers to the first emigration. As for the second emigration to Abyssinia, it was, as Al-Waqidi claimed, in the fifth year after the mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). "To my Lord" means: to the pleasure of my Lord and to wherever He commanded me.

(Indeed, He is the Mighty, the Wise.) This has already been discussed. The discussion of emigration has also been covered in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 349 and following, first or second edition.]] and elsewhere. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him Isaac﴾, meaning: Allah bestowed children upon him, so He gave him Isaac as a son, and Jacob as a grandson. Isaac was given to him after Ishmael, and Jacob came from Isaac.

(And We placed in his offspring prophethood and the Book.) Allah did not send any prophet after Abraham except from his lineage. The word "Book" is in the singular because it is intended as a verbal noun, like "prophethood," and what is meant is the Torah and the Gospel [and the Furqan]. Thus it is an expression for the plural. The Torah was revealed to Moses from the descendants of Abraham, the Gospel to Jesus from his descendants, and the Furqan to Muhammad (ﷺ) from his descendants, peace be upon them all.

(And We gave him his reward in this world.) This means the consensus of the adherents of all religions upon him. This was said by Ikrimah. Sufyan narrated from Humayd ibn Qays, who said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr instructed a man to ask Ikrimah about the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾. Ikrimah said: The people of all religions claim him and say he is one of them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: He has spoken the truth. Qatadah said: It is like His saying, ﴿And We gave him in this world a good reputation﴾, meaning a good outcome, righteous deeds, and a fine praise. This is because the people of every religion take him as their own. It was also said: ﴿We gave him his reward in this world﴾ means that most of the prophets are from his offspring.

(And indeed, in the Hereafter, he is among the righteous.) "In the Hereafter" is not part of the relative clause; rather it is an explanation. Its explanation has already passed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 133, second edition.]]. All of this is an exhortation to follow the example of Abraham in patience upon the true religion.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: The meaning is "And We delivered Lot" or "We sent Lot." He said: This interpretation is more beloved to me. It is also permissible that the meaning is "Remember Lot, when he said to his people, rebuking or warning them": ﴿Indeed, you commit an abomination that no one in the worlds has preceded you in.﴾ The reading of "a-innakum" (whether the second hamza is pronounced) has been mentioned here and its explanation in surah al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 245 and following, first or second edition.]]. The story of Lot and his people has also preceded in al-A'raf and Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 79, first or second edition.]].

﴿And you cut off the road﴾. It was said: They were highway robbers; this was said by Ibn Zayd. It was also said: They would seize people from the roads for the purpose of committing the abomination; this was related by Ibn Shajarah. And it was said: It is the cutting off of offspring by turning away from women to men; this was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih, meaning they became content with men instead of women. I say: Perhaps all of this was among them, so they would rob travellers of their wealth and commit the abomination, and they would dispense with women through that.

﴿And you commit in your gatherings the evil﴾. Al-nadi (the gathering) is the assembly. The people differed about the evil they used to commit in it. One group said: They would pelt women with pebbles and mock the stranger and the passer-by. Umm Hani narrated this from the Prophet (ﷺ). Umm Hani said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And you commit in your gatherings the evil﴾. He said: "They would pelt whoever passed by them with pebbles and mock him, and that is the evil they used to commit." Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related it in his Musnad, and al-Nahhas, al-Tha'labi, al-Mahdawi and al-Mawardi mentioned it.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned: Mu'awiyah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The people of Lot used to sit in their assemblies, and beside each man was a bowl containing pebbles for pelting. When a passer-by came to them, they would throw at him, and whichever of them hit him had the greater right to him," meaning he would take him for the abomination. That is His saying: ﴿And you commit in your gatherings the evil﴾.

Aisha, Ibn Abbas, al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah [[With a fatha on the ba' and a shaddah on the zay, as in al-Taqrib.]] and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: They used to break wind (yatadarratun) in their assemblies. Mujahid [[In all the copies: Mujahid and Mansur. The "tasweit" (vocalizing) is from the tafsir of al-Tabari and others.]] and Mansur said: They would have intercourse with men in their assemblies while some of them looked at others. It is also from Mujahid: Among their affairs were pigeon-racing, dyeing the fingertips with henna, whistling, pelting with pebbles, and abandoning modesty in all their affairs. Ibn Atiyyah said: These matters may be found among some of the disobedient of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), so forbidding them is obligatory. Makhul said: In this community there are ten of the characteristics of the people of Lot: chewing gum, dyeing the fingers with henna, loosening the waistwrap, cracking the knuckles [[Tanqid al-asabi' means cracking them.]], the turban wound around the head, interlacing (of fingers), throwing the slingshot [[Al-julahiq is the pellet-bow by which pellets are thrown. Al-khadhf with a dotted kha' means pelting with it.]], whistling, pelting, and sodomy.

From Ibn Abbas, he said: The people of Lot had sins other than the abomination, among them that they oppressed one another, cursed one another, broke wind in their assemblies, pelted with pebbles, played backgammon and chess, wore dyed garments, made their roosters fight and their rams butt, dyed their fingers with henna, men imitated women's clothing and women imitated men's clothing, they imposed tolls on every passer-by, and despite all this they associated partners with Allah. They were the first upon whose hands sodomy and lesbianism appeared. When Lot, peace be upon him, confronted them with these abominations, they returned to denial and obstinacy, and said: ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah﴾, meaning that such a thing would not occur and he had no power over it. They only said this while firmly believing him to be a liar. It is not sound in human nature that an obstinate person would say this and then Lot, peace be upon him, sought help from his Lord, so He sent angels against them for their punishment. They came first to Abraham bringing good tidings of the victory of Lot over his people, as has been explained earlier in Hud and elsewhere.

Al-A'mash, Ya'qub, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿li-nunjiyahu wa-ahlahu﴾ with lightening (takhfif). The rest read it with emphasis (tashdid). Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿Innā munjūka wa-ahlaka﴾ with lightening, and the rest with emphasis. These are two dialects: anja and najja have the same meaning, and this has preceded. Ibn Amir read ﴿Innā munazzilūn﴾ with emphasis, and this is the reading of Ibn Abbas; the rest read it with lightening.

His saying: ﴿And We have left from it a clear sign for a people who reason﴾. Qatadah said: It is the stones that were left, and Abu al-Aliyah said the same. It was also said: A people from this community are stoned with them. Ibn Abbas said: It is the traces of their ruined dwellings. Mujahid said: It is the black water on the surface of the earth. All of these remain, so there is no contradiction.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 29, verse 38:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [We destroyed] ʿAd and Thamud﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: Some of them said it refers back to the beginning of the surah, meaning: "And We certainly tested those before them, and We tested ʿAd and Thamud." He said: "What is more beloved to me is that it be conjoined to ﴿So the quake seized them﴾, and [that it means] 'the [punishment] seized ʿAd and Thamud.'" Al-Zajjaj claimed that the implied meaning is "and We destroyed ʿAd and Thamud." It was also said: The meaning is, "Remember ʿAd, when We sent to them Hud, and they denied him, so We destroyed them; and Thamud too, We sent to them Salih, and they denied him, so We destroyed them with the Blast, just as We destroyed ʿAd with the barren wind."

(﴿And it has become clear to you﴾), O assembly of the disbelievers, ﴿from their dwellings﴾ at al-Hijr and al-Ahqaf, ﴿signs﴾ of their destruction. The agent of "became clear" has been omitted.

(﴿And Satan made their deeds appealing to them﴾), that is, their vile deeds, so they considered them lofty.

(﴿And he barred them from the path﴾), that is, from the way of truth.

(﴿And they were discerning﴾). Regarding this there are two views. One: "and they were discerning within error," related from Mujahid. The second: "they were discerning, having recognized truth from falsehood through the manifest proofs." This second view is more fitting, because one says "so-and-so is discerning" only when he knows a matter as it truly is. Al-Farra' said: "They were intelligent people possessing insight, but their insight did not benefit them." It was also said: "They committed what they committed while it had already become clear to them that their end would be punishment."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 29, verse 39–40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Qarun and Pharaoh and Haman﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: If you wish, it is governed by ʿAd, and there is in it what there is in it; and if you wish, it is governed by "and He barred them from the way," and [He barred] Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman. It was also said: that is, We destroyed these after their messengers had come to them, (and they waxed arrogant in the land) against the truth and against the worship of Allah.

(And they were not ones who could escape) — that is, they could not escape. It was also said: [they were not] outstripping [Us] in disbelief; rather, many generations had preceded them in disbelief, and We destroyed them.

(So each We seized for his sin.) Al-Kisa'i said: "each" (kullan) is in the accusative, governed by "We seized" (akhadhna), meaning: We seized each one for his sin.

(Among them were those upon whom We sent a violent wind with pebbles.) This refers to the people of Lut. The ḥāṣib (violent wind) is a wind that brings small pebbles, namely small stones; and it is used for every punishment. (Among them were those seized by the Cry.) This refers to Thamud and the people of Madyan.

(Among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow.) This refers to Qarun. (Among them were those whom We drowned.) [This refers to] the people of Nuh and the people of Pharaoh.

(And Allah was not one to wrong them.) Because He warned them, gave them respite, sent messengers to them, and removed every excuse.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 29, verses 41–43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The parable of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider's,﴾ al-Akhfash said: "like the spider's" is a complete pause (waqf tamm), and then he begins the story of it, saying: (it takes a house). Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an error, because "it takes a house" is a relative clause (silah) describing the spider, as if he had said: like that of the one (female) which takes a house. So it is not good to pause on the relative clause without the relative pronoun it modifies. It is comparable to His saying: "like the donkey that carries books" (yahmilu asfara), where "yahmilu" is a relative clause describing the donkey, and it is not good to pause on "the donkey" without "yahmilu."

Al-Farra' said: It is a parable which Allah, glorified is He, struck for one who takes other than Him as gods that neither benefit nor harm him, just as the spider's house does not protect her from heat or cold. And it is not good to pause on "the spider," because when the comparison intended her house, which protects her from nothing, the gods that neither benefit nor harm were likened to it.

(And indeed the weakest of houses) i.e., the most feeble of houses (is the spider's house). Al-Dahhak said: He struck this parable for the weakness and feebleness of their gods, likening them to the spider's house.

(If only they knew.) "Law" (if only) is connected to the spider's house, i.e., if they knew that worshipping idols is like taking the spider's house, which does not avail them anything, and that this is their parable when they worship them; not that they know the spider's house is weak.

The grammarians said: The taa' at the end of "al-'ankabut" is an augmentation (zaa'idah), because it drops in the diminutive and the plural, and the word is feminine. Al-Farra' related its use as masculine and recited:

"Over their high ground, among them are houses, as if the spider had built them."

It is also transmitted as:

"Over Ahtaluhum, among them are houses."

Al-Jawhari said: Al-Hattal is the name of a mountain. Al-'Ankabut is the well-known small creature that weaves a thin, loose web in the air. Its plurals are 'anakib, 'anakib, 'ikab, 'ukub and 'a'kub. It is also reported that one says "ankab" and "ankabah" (with the nun placed before the kaf), and the poet said:

"As if there falls from its foam
a spider's house in its time."

Its diminutive is "unaykib." It is related from Yazid ibn Maysarah that the spider is a devil whom Allah transformed. Ata al-Khurasani said: The spider wove twice: once over Dawud when Jalut was seeking him, and once over the Prophet (ﷺ), and for this reason its killing was forbidden. It is related from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: Clean your houses of spider webs, for leaving them in the houses brings poverty, and withholding the leaven brings poverty.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah knows whatever they call upon besides Him of anything.﴾ "Ma" here means "alladhi" (that which), and "min" is partitive (lil-tab'id). Had it been an emphatic extra particle, the meaning would have been reversed. The meaning is: Allah knows the weakness of what they worship besides Him. ʿĀṣim, Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub read "yad'una" with the ya' (they call upon), and this is the preference of Abu ʿUbayd, because the nations before them are mentioned. The rest read it with the ta' (you call upon), addressing them directly.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And these parables We strike for the people, but none understands them except the knowledgeable.﴾ i.e., this parable and others mentioned in al-Baqarah, al-Hajj and elsewhere, "We strike them" means "We clarify them" for the people, "and none understands them" means none comprehends them, "except the knowledgeable," i.e., those who know Allah, as Jabir reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The knowledgeable one is he who understands from Allah, then acts in obedience to Him and avoids His displeasure."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And these parables We strike for the people, but none understands them except the knowledgeable.﴾ i.e., this parable and others mentioned in al-Baqarah, al-Hajj and elsewhere, "We strike them" means "We clarify them" for the people, "and none understands them" means none comprehends them, "except the knowledgeable," i.e., those who know Allah, as Jabir reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The knowledgeable one is he who understands from Allah, then acts in obedience to Him and avoids His displeasure."

Allah's saying: ﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾, that is, with justice and equity. It was also said: with His word and His power, and that is the truth.

(Indeed in that is a sign) that is, an indication and a proof (for the believers), those who affirm.

**The first issue:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Recite﴾, an imperative from *tilawa* (recitation) and from persevering in it. The threat against those who turn away from it has already been mentioned in *Surat Ta-Ha* [[See vol. 1, p. 258 onward, first or second edition.]], and the command to urge people toward it was mentioned in the introduction to this book [[See vol. 1, p. ___ onward, second or third edition.]]. "The Book" here refers to the Qur'an.

**The second issue:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ and to his community. To establish the prayer means to perform it at its proper time, with its recitation, bowing, prostration, sitting, tashahhud, and all its conditions. This has already been explained in *al-Baqara* [[See vol. 1, p. 164 onward, second or third edition.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

**The third issue:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾. This means that the five daily prayers are what expiate the sins committed between them, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Tell me, if there were a river at the door of one of you in which he bathed five times every day, would any of his dirt remain?" They said: "No dirt would remain on him." He said: "That is the likeness of the five prayers; through them Allah erases sins." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and said of it: "It is a hasan sahih hadith."

Ibn Umar said: "Here, 'the prayer' means the Qur'an." The meaning is that what is recited in the prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing, and prohibits adultery and sins.

I say: Among this is the sahih hadith: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves," meaning the recitation of al-Fatiha.

Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, Ibn Jurayj and al-Kalbi said: "As long as the servant is in his prayer, he does not commit immorality or wrongdoing." That is, the prayer prohibits as long as you are in it.

Ibn Atiyya said: "This is a non-Arabic (foreign) interpretation. How does this compare with what Anas ibn Malik narrated? He said: 'There was a young man among the Ansar who prayed with the Prophet ﷺ, but he did not leave any of the indecencies or theft without committing it. This was mentioned to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "Indeed, the prayer will prohibit him." He did not delay before he repented and his condition improved.' Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Did I not tell you?'"

There is a third interpretation of the verse, which the scholars of verification (*al-muhaqqiqun*) have approved, which the Sufi shaykhs have held, and which the commentators have mentioned. It is said that "establish the prayer" means to continue it and to uphold its limits. Then He informed of a ruling from Him: that the prayer prohibits its performer and its practitioner from immorality and wrongdoing. This is because it contains the recitation of the Qur'an, which includes admonition. The prayer occupies the whole body of the one praying. When the one praying enters his place of worship, becomes humble, submits to his Lord, and remembers that he is standing before Him, that He is watching over him and sees him, his soul becomes fit for this and humbled. The awareness of Allah the Exalted pervades it, and its awe appears on his limbs. He does not slacken from this until another prayer shades him, by which he returns to the best state. This is the meaning of these reports, because the prayer of the believer should be like this.

I say: Especially if he makes himself aware that this might be the last of his deeds. This is more effective in the intended purpose and more complete in the meaning, for death has no fixed age, no specific time, and no known illness. This is something on which there is no disagreement.

It is narrated from some of the early Muslims (*salaf*) that whenever he stood to pray, he would tremble and his color would turn pale. He was questioned about this and said: "I am standing before Allah the Exalted. It is fitting for me to feel this before the kings of this world, so how much more before the King of kings?"

This is a prayer that will certainly prohibit immorality and wrongdoing. But whoever's prayer revolves around merely being valid, with no humility, no remembrance, and no virtues, like our prayer (and would that it were valid), that prayer leaves its performer in his station wherever he is. If he is on a path of sins that distance him from Allah the Exalted, the prayer leaves him to persist in his distance.

On this basis is understood the hadith reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-A'mash, who said: "Whoever his prayer does not restrain from immorality and wrongdoing, it will increase him in distance from Allah and nothing else." It has been narrated that al-Hasan transmitted it as a mursal report from the Prophet ﷺ, but that is not of sound chain.

Ibn Atiyya said: "I heard my father, may Allah be pleased with him, say: 'When we have established this and examined its meaning, it is not permissible to say that the prayer of the disobedient person itself distances him from Allah, as if it were a sin. Rather, it is understood that it does not bring him closer to Allah, but leaves him in his state and his sins, from immorality, wrongdoing and distance. So the prayer only confirms that distance which was his way. It is as if it distanced him, since it did not restrain his distance from Allah.'"

It was said to Ibn Mas'ud: "So-and-so prays a lot." He said: "It does not benefit anyone except the one who obeys it."

I say: In general, the meaning intended by the hadith "it will increase him in distance from Allah, and he will only increase in hatred from Allah through it" is an indication that the one who commits immorality and wrongdoing has no value in his prayer, because sins dominate its doer.

It has been said: this is a report with the meaning of a command, i.e., let the one praying refrain from immorality and wrongdoing. The prayer by itself does not prohibit, but it is the cause of refraining. This is like His saying: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with the truth﴾, and His saying: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾

**The fourth issue:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾. That is, Allah's remembrance of you with reward and praise is greater than your remembrance of Him in your worship and prayers. This was the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Darda, Abu Qurra, Salman and al-Hasan, and it is the view chosen by al-Tabari.

It has been narrated as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) from the hadith of Musa ibn Uqba from Nafi from Ibn Umar that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "And the remembrance of Allah is greater," he said: "The remembrance of Allah of you is greater than your remembrance of Him."

It has been said: your remembrance of Allah in your prayer and in the recitation of the Qur'an is better than everything else.

It has been said: the meaning is that the remembrance of Allah, together with consistency in the prayer, is greater in prohibiting immorality and wrongdoing.

Al-Dahhak said: "And the remembrance of Allah during ihram (the pilgrim's state), so he leaves the most sublime remembrance." 

It has been said: the meaning is that the remembrance of Allah for the prohibition of immorality and wrongdoing is greater, i.e., *kabir* (great). The word *akbar* can have the meaning of *kabir*.

Ibn Zayd and Qatada said: "And the remembrance of Allah is greater than everything," meaning it is better than all acts of worship without remembrance.

It has been said: the remembrance of Allah prevents disobedience, for whoever is mindful of Him does not oppose Him.

Ibn Atiyya said: "In my view, the meaning is that the remembrance of Allah is greater in absolute terms; that is, it is what prohibits immorality and wrongdoing. The part of it that occurs in the prayer does this, and it does the same outside the prayer, because refraining only comes from one who remembers Allah and is watchful of Him."

The reward for this is that Allah the Exalted remembers him, as in the hadith: "Whoever remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; and whoever remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than theirs." The movements of the prayer have no effect in prohibiting anything. The beneficial remembrance is that which is with knowledge, with the heart turned toward Allah and free for Him alone. As for what does not go beyond the tongue, it is of a different rank.

The remembrance of Allah the Exalted toward the servant is the outpouring of guidance and the light of knowledge upon him, and this is the fruit of the servant's remembrance of his Lord. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So remember Me; I will remember you﴾.

The rest of the verse is a form of warning and an exhortation to watchfulness.

There are two issues here.

The first concerns God's words, "And do not argue with the People of the Scripture except in a way that is best." Scholars differed over it. Mujahid said it is *muhkam* (definitive, not abrogated). Therefore it is permissible to argue with the People of the Scripture in the best manner, meaning by calling them to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and by drawing their attention to His proofs and signs, in the hope that they will respond by believing. It must not be done in a harsh or coarse way. On this view, His words "except those of them who did wrong" mean those who wronged you. Otherwise, all of them are wrongdoers absolutely. It was also said: the meaning is, do not argue with those of the People of the Scripture who believed in Muhammad ﷺ, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and those who believed with him.

"Except in a way that is best" means: by agreeing with what they tell you of the reports about their earlier generations and other matters. On this interpretation, His words "except those who did wrong" refer to those among them who remained in their disbelief, such as those of Qurayza and al-Nadir and others who disbelieved and betrayed. On this view too, the verse is *muhkam*. It was also said that this verse is *mansukh* (abrogated, i.e. its ruling has been superseded) by the verse of fighting, God's words: "Fight those who do not believe in Allah." Qatada said: "except those who did wrong" means those who ascribed a son to Allah and said, "The hand of Allah is chained" and "Allah is poor." These are the polytheists who waged war and did not pay the *jizya* (poll tax), so they were defeated. Al-Nahhas and others said: whoever holds that it is abrogated argues that the verse is Meccan, and at that time there was no obligatory fighting, no demand for the *jizya*, and nothing else of that kind. The view of Mujahid is good, because the rulings of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are not said to be abrogated except by a report that removes all excuse, or by a proof from reason. Ibn al-Arabi chose this view.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: His words "except those of them who did wrong" mean: except those who waged war against the believers, so arguing with them is by the sword until they believe or pay the *jizya*.

The second issue concerns God's words, "And say: We believe in what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to you." Al-Bukhari related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The People of the Scripture used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it in Arabic to the people of Islam. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not believe the People of the Scripture and do not disbelieve them, and say: 'We believe in what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to you.'" 

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not ask the People of the Scripture about anything, for they will not guide you, and they have gone astray. Either you will deny something true, or you will affirm something false."

In al-Bukhari: from Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman, who heard Mu'awiya relating to a group of Quraysh in Medina, and he mentioned Ka'b al-Ahbar, saying: "He is one of the most truthful of these narrators who narrate from the People of the Scripture, although even so, we test him for lies."
